Section 50 Licences

Street works licences for non-statutory undertakers — what they are, what conditions apply, and what happens when things go wrong.

📖 What is a Section 50 licence?
NRSWA 1991 s.50 & Schedule 3 — the basics
›
💬 Plain English

Utility companies — gas, water, electricity, telecoms — have a statutory right to dig up roads. They don't need anyone's permission — they just notify and get on with it. Everyone else who wants to put something in the highway needs to ask. That asking is a Section 50 licence.

Common examples: a housing developer connecting to the sewer, a private landowner installing a private water supply, a business running a duct between two premises, an EV chargepoint installer (without SWA code powers), a private resident connecting a drainage run.

Once the licence is granted, the licensee becomes an undertaker for the purposes of NRSWA — meaning all the same duties, obligations and penalties apply to them as to a utility company. They can't claim ignorance of the rules by saying "we're not a utility."

Who needs a s.50 licence?
Anyone without statutory right to install apparatus in the highway
Who does NOT need one?
Statutory undertakers (gas/water/electricity/telecoms) — they use permits instead
What can be licensed?
Pipes, ducts, cables, drains, chambers, culverts — any apparatus in the highway
Who grants the licence?
The highway authority — not the permit authority
Minimum notice period
Typically 21 working days before works start (varies by authority)
Working without a licence
Criminal offence — liable to prosecution
Liability
Cannot be delegated — the licensee remains liable even if a contractor does the work
📌 A s.50 licence is NOT a permit. Statutory undertakers use permits (via Street Manager). S.50 licences are issued directly by the highway authority — some authorities use Street Manager to register them voluntarily, but this is not mandatory.
⚖️ S.50 Licensee vs Statutory Undertaker — Key Differences
Same obligations, different route in — important distinctions
›
💬 Plain English

Think of it this way: a utility company has a legal right to dig up your road — they don't need to ask. They just tell you when. A s.50 licensee has no such right — they're a guest on the highway, not a resident. They had to ask permission and pay for the privilege. But once they're in, the rules are identical. The same SROH, the same FPNs, the same overrun charges. The only extra layer is the bond — security money held by the HA in case things go wrong — and the HA's power to refuse or put conditions on the licence in a way they can't with a statutory undertaker.

On site this matters because a s.50 licensee may genuinely not know the rules. A gas engineer is NRSWA-trained as a matter of course. A private developer doing a single sewer connection may never have heard of the SROH. That's not a defence — but it explains why inspections on s.50 sites often find more basic compliance failures.

📌 The key practical difference on site: a statutory undertaker's team won't have a s.50 licence — they'll have a permit reference. A s.50 site should have the licence visible (many authorities require it to be on site). If you can't find the licence or permit reference — that's worth investigating.
📝 Before Works Start — Licence Requirements
What must be in place before a single shovel goes in
›
💬 Plain English

A s.50 licence isn't like a building regulation approval that you get once and forget. It's a live permission that has specific conditions attached, and those conditions have to be met before the first cone goes out. The most common failure on s.50 sites is a contractor arriving on site without the licence having been issued — or with the licence but without the right people or insurance. The licence is not just paperwork — it's the legal basis for every person and every piece of equipment on that site.

If a site is running without a valid licence in place, or before the licensed start date — that's not an FPN situation, it's a criminal offence. The HA can direct works to stop immediately.

Application timingMinimum notice required
21 working days minimum before start (varies by authority — check licence)
Public liability insuranceMinimum cover
£5 million minimum — must cover from start to acceptance of permanent reinstatement
Qualified operativeOn site at all times
NRSWA-qualified operative required on site at all times during works
Qualified supervisor
NRSWA-qualified supervisor to oversee works
Scale planSubmitted with application
1:500 or greater showing location and depth of proposed apparatus
Traffic management plan
Proposed TM method submitted with application — Chapter 8 compliant
Bond / deposit
Paid in advance — amount varies by area and depth (see Bond section below)
Other servicesBefore starting
Licensee must contact all affected public undertakers and obtain records of existing apparatus
Information board on site
Required — contractor name, duration, licence/permit ref, 24/7 contact number
📌 Works must not start until the licence has been issued. If works are found to have started before the licence was granted — that's a criminal offence. The licence is the permission to work. Check the licence start date against the date works commenced on site.
📜 Licence Conditions — What They Typically Require
Schedule 3 NRSWA — HA may attach conditions as they consider appropriate
›
💬 Plain English

Under Schedule 3 of NRSWA, the highway authority can attach any conditions to a s.50 licence that it considers appropriate. This is broad — they can restrict working hours, require specific reinstatement specs, impose supervision requirements, require photos, and more. Conditions vary between authorities. The licence document itself is the authority — always check what conditions have been attached to the specific licence you're looking at.

Working hoursTypical condition
08:00–18:00 Mon–Fri — no works outside these hours without HA permission
Reinstatement spec
SROH mandatory — same as any other street works
Completion notification
By end of next working day after permanent reinstatement — or by 10:00 next day if completed after 16:30
As-built drawing
1:500 OS plan showing precise location of apparatus — accuracy ±300mm with co-ordinates
Reinstatement photos
Many authorities require photos submitted with completion notice — time/date stamped
Consequential damage
Reinstatement must include any area the HA considers to have suffered consequential damage
Start/end date adherence
Must notify HA immediately if start date changes — FPN risk if works start outside licensed dates
Breach of conditions
FPN may be issued for breach of any licence condition
📌 The licence conditions are not optional extras — they're part of the legal permission. A licensee who doesn't follow the conditions is in breach of the licence, which can result in FPNs and in serious cases revocation of the licence itself.
🛣️ Reinstatement Obligations
Same as NRSWA — SROH mandatory, guarantee period applies
›
💬 Plain English

There is no "lighter touch" reinstatement standard for s.50 work. A private developer reinstating a carriageway trench must do it exactly the same way as a utility company — same materials, same depths, same tolerances, same edge preparation. The SROH does not have a section for small companies or one-off jobs. If the road was Type 1 before the excavation, it has to be Type 1 when they leave.

The guarantee period works differently from a utility's regime. On a s.50 site the HA typically carries out three programmed inspections: one during works, one after permanent reinstatement, and one near the end of the guarantee period. These are part of the licence fee. The licensee knows they're coming — or should. If the reinstatement fails at the Cat C inspection, the bond pays for the repairs.

💬 Plain English

The reinstatement requirements for a s.50 licensee are identical to those for a statutory undertaker. The SROH applies in full. There is no reduced standard because the licensee is a private individual or small company. The inspector's job on a s.50 site is exactly the same as on any other street works site — check the materials, the layers, the tolerances, the edge preparation.

Reinstatement standard
SROH — full specification applies, no exceptions
Guarantee period — standard
2 years from date HA notified of permanent reinstatement
Guarantee period — deepExcavation >1.5m
3 years from date HA notified of permanent reinstatement
Interim to permanentTime limit
6 months maximum for interim reinstatement (SROH standard timescales)
Qualified operatives
NRSWA-qualified operatives required — same as statutory undertakers
Reinstatement detailsNotification
SWL4 form (or equivalent) within 10 working days of reinstatement — including dimensions and photos
Defect found during guarantee
Licensee liable for all repair costs — deducted from bond if not remedied
📌 One key difference from statutory undertakers: on a s.50 site the HA typically carries out a defined number of inspections (Cat A during works, Cat B after permanent reinstatement, Cat C near end of guarantee) as part of the licence fee. These are not random sample inspections — they're programmed. The licensee should know they're coming.
💰 The Bond / Deposit System
Refundable security held by HA for duration of guarantee period
›
💬 Plain English

Before works start, the licensee pays a bond — a refundable deposit held by the highway authority. It's security against the reinstatement failing or the licensee walking away from their obligations. If the reinstatement is defective and the licensee doesn't fix it, the HA can use the bond to pay for the repairs. If everything is fine at the end of the guarantee period, the bond is returned in full.

Bond amounts vary significantly between authorities. They're based on the size and depth of the excavation. Deep excavations (over 1.5m) carry a higher bond because they have longer guarantee periods and higher risk of failure.

Bond — typical small opening<5m² <1.5m deep
~£1,000 (varies by authority)
Bond — medium opening5–10m² <1.5m deep
~£1,500
Bond — medium opening5–10m² >1.5m deep
~£2,500
Bond — larger opening10–30m² >1.5m deep
~£3,500
When bond is returned
After satisfactory Cat C inspection — 23 months (or 35 months for deep) after permanent reinstatement
Deductions from bond
Defect inspection costs, remedial works costs — deducted before return
Bond vs FPNImportant distinction
Bond deductions are civil — separate from FPNs which remain available for criminal offences
📌 Bond amounts shown above are illustrative — they vary significantly between authorities. Some authorities don't require bonds at all (the DfT guidance says this is a matter for each authority). Always check the specific licence for the bond amount and conditions.
🔍 Inspection Rights & Powers
s.72 & s.75 NRSWA — same powers as for any undertaker
›
💬 Plain English

The authority's inspection powers under NRSWA apply to s.50 licensees in exactly the same way as to statutory undertakers. The inspector has the right to inspect the works at any stage — during excavation, during reinstatement, and throughout the guarantee period. The licensee cannot refuse an inspection.

Inspection power
s.72 NRSWA — authority may inspect, investigate and report on works and reinstatements at any time
Cat A inspectionDuring works
Signing, lighting, guarding, excavation method, reinstatement in progress
Cat B inspectionAfter permanent reinstatement
Immediately after permanent reinstatement is complete — material, level, finish
Cat C inspectionEnd of guarantee
One month before end of guarantee period — check for settlement, cracking, edge depression
Inspection fee
£50 per inspection unit (based on works duration) — typically included in licence fee for standard 3-inspection programme
Defect inspection fee
£120 per follow-up inspection to check defect has been repaired
Investigatory worksCoring etc.
Authority may carry out investigatory works (coring) at any time — licensee bears cost if non-compliant
Remedial works by HA
If defect not remedied — HA may carry out works and recover costs from bond or licensee direct
📌 On a s.50 site the inspector's role is identical to any other street works inspection. Check: is the licence on site or referenced? Are operatives NRSWA-qualified? Is the TM compliant with Chapter 8? Is the reinstatement to SROH? The licence doesn't create a different standard — it creates the same standard for someone who wouldn't otherwise be subject to it.
⚠️ Penalties, Charges & Enforcement
Same FPNs, same s.74 overrun charges — and bond deductions on top
›
💬 Plain English

The penalty exposure on a s.50 site is often more surprising to the licensee than to the inspector. A small developer who expected a quick drain connection can find themselves facing FPNs for signing failures, overrun charges of thousands of pounds per day, defect inspection fees, bond deductions, and potentially a prosecution if they worked without the licence or before it was issued. The liability cannot be passed to the contractor — the licensee's name is on the licence and they wear every consequence.

This is also why inspectors need to be thorough on s.50 sites. A utility company has a compliance department and legal team. A private developer may not even know what an FPN is. The fact that they didn't know the rules doesn't reduce the penalty — but it might explain why the failures are basic ones.

💬 Plain English

A s.50 licensee faces exactly the same FPN regime as a statutory undertaker — the same offences, the same penalties. On top of that, they also have the bond at risk. And on top of that, the HA can refuse or revoke the licence for serious non-compliance. In practice this means a small developer or private individual can face substantial costs for getting it wrong — often more than the works cost in the first place.

FPNs available
All 28 standard FPNs apply — s.54, s.55, s.57, s.59, s.65, s.70, s.74 etc.
Working without licence
Criminal offence — prosecution, not FPN
Breach of licence conditions
FPN — £2,500 / £1,875 discounted. Can also trigger licence review.
S.74 overrun charges
Yes — full charge table applies. Can be £10,000/day on a Cat 0/1 TS road.
Reinstatement defect
C10/C11/C18 defect notices — repair within timeframe or HA remediates and recovers costs from bond
Licence revocation
HA may revoke licence for serious or persistent non-compliance
Liability delegation
Cannot delegate — licensee remains liable even if contractor is at fault
📌 The "I didn't know" defence doesn't work. The GOV.UK guidance is explicit that those not familiar with NRSWA requirements should appoint a contractor with appropriate knowledge. Ignorance of the rules is not a mitigation — it's a reason why the bond and licence conditions exist.
🔄 S.50 vs Permit Scheme — Key Differences
For areas operating a permit scheme — what changes for s.50 works
›
💬 Plain English

In a permit scheme area, statutory undertakers apply for permits through Street Manager before every job. S.50 licensees don't use Street Manager permits in the same way — they have a licence issued directly by the HA. However, the HA may voluntarily register the s.50 works in Street Manager for co-ordination purposes, and the licensee may still need to observe permit conditions around timing, road space, and traffic-sensitive streets.

Permit requirement
S.50 licensees do not apply for permits via Street Manager — licence is the permission
Street Manager registration
HA may voluntarily register s.50 works in Street Manager — but this is not mandatory for licensee
Co-ordination duty
S.50 works must still be co-ordinated — HA has network management duty under TMA 2004
Traffic-sensitive streets
HA can impose conditions restricting working times on TS streets — same as permit conditions
Protected streets
HA may refuse or impose enhanced conditions on protected streets
Lane rentalWhere operating
S.74A lane rental applies to s.50 licensees in the same way as statutory undertakers where a lane rental scheme operates
Works register
HA must keep a record of all s.50 licences on the Street Works Register
📌 If you're inspecting a s.50 site in a permit scheme area and the works aren't visible in Street Manager — that's not necessarily a breach. The HA may have registered them or they may simply not be on Street Manager. Check with the HA whether they register s.50 works and what reference system they use.
✅ Quick Check — Inspecting a S.50 Site
What to check when you arrive at a s.50 licence site
›
1. Licence on site / reference visible?

Ask for the s.50 licence or licence reference number. Works cannot start without a licence. If they can't produce a reference — check with the HA. Working without a licence = criminal offence.

2. NRSWA-qualified operative on site?

Required at all times during works. Ask for their Street Works Qualification card. If no qualified operative = C8 (failure to have qualified person on site).

3. Works within licensed dates and hours?

Check licence start and end date. Check time — typically 08:00–18:00 unless HA has permitted otherwise. Works outside licensed dates or hours = breach of conditions = FPN.

4. TM compliant with Chapter 8?

Same Chapter 8 requirements as any other street works. Check signing, lighting, guarding, safety zone, cone spacings. C-series offences apply.

5. Information board on site?

Must show contractor name, licence duration, contact details including 24/7 emergency number. Missing = C3 (failure to display information board).

6. Reinstatement to SROH?

Full SROH applies. Check materials, layer depths, edge preparation, tolerances. Same inspection as any other reinstatement. Defect = C10/C11/C18.

⚠️ Grey area — licence conditions vary

Conditions attached to s.50 licences vary significantly between authorities. Before issuing an FPN for a condition breach, confirm what conditions are actually attached to THIS specific licence. Don't assume standard conditions apply — read the licence.

Based on NRSWA 1991 s.50 & Schedule 3, TMA 2004, and GOV.UK guidance (updated March 2026). Licence conditions vary between highway authorities — always check the specific licence.

⚖️ Penalty Amounts

›
  • £2,500 Statutory undertaker — most NRSWA offences
  • £500 Permit — working without / outside permit
  • £500 Conditions — failure to comply
  • £2,500 Conditions — where mandatory FPN applies
⚠️ Discount = 25% if paid within 29 days of issue

📅 Key Time Limits

›
  • 91 days Maximum to issue FPN from date of offence
  • 29 days Discount payment window from date FPN issued
  • 29 days Payment deadline before prosecution considered
⚠️ The 91-day limit is absolute — cannot be extended

📋 FPN Issue Checklist

›
  • 1. Confirm offence and section reference
  • 2. Check 91-day window has not expired
  • 3. Identify the correct undertaker / permit holder
  • 4. Take photographic evidence of the breach
  • 5. Record exact location, USRN, coordinates if possible
  • 6. Note works reference / permit reference
  • 7. Issue FPN — original to undertaker, copy retained
  • 8. Log in your authority's FPN register

NRSWA 1991 — Statutory Sections

📖 s.54 — Advance notice of works

›
💬 Plain English

Before a utility company digs up the road they must warn the council in advance. For most jobs that's at least 10 working days' notice. For big jobs it's 3 months. Only genuine emergencies are exempt. If they just start digging without telling anyone — that's this offence.

NRSWA 1991 s.54
Advance notice of certain works

(1) Before beginning to execute any street works to which this section applies, the undertaker shall give the street authority such advance notice as may be prescribed of his intention to execute the works.

(2) This section applies to street works which are not emergency works.

(3) The notice shall be given not less than the prescribed period before the works begin.

Minimum notice: 10 working days (standard), 3 months (major works). Emergency works exempt — s.57 applies instead.
⚠️ FPN: £2,500 full / £1,875 discounted (pay within 29 days)

📖 s.55 — Notice of actual start date

›
💬 Plain English

Even after giving advance notice the company must confirm the actual date they're starting. If they turn up earlier than they said — or move the job forward without telling the council — that's this offence. Think of it as the second notification: "we told you we were coming, now here's the exact date."

NRSWA 1991 s.55
Notice of starting date of works

(1) An undertaker who has given notice under section 54 shall give the street authority notice of the date on which the works are to begin, not less than the prescribed period before that date.

(2) If the works are not begun on the notified date, the undertaker shall give fresh notice under this section.

(3) An undertaker who begins works without giving notice as required by this section, or before the notified date, is guilty of an offence and liable to a fixed penalty notice.

Commonly triggered when a job is brought forward without updating the street authority. A fresh notice is required any time the start date changes.
⚠️ FPN: £2,500 full / £1,875 discounted (pay within 29 days)

📖 s.57 — Notice of emergency works

›
💬 Plain English

If there's a burst pipe or cable emergency the company can start digging straight away — that's fine. But they still have to phone the council as soon as they possibly can after starting and explain why it's an emergency. Forgetting to call, or doing it hours later with no good reason, is this offence.

NRSWA 1991 s.57
Notice of emergency works

(1) An undertaker who executes emergency works shall, as soon as reasonably practicable after commencing the works, give the street authority notice of— (a) the place and nature of the works, and (b) the reason for treating the works as emergency works.

(2) An undertaker who fails to comply with subsection (1) is guilty of an offence and liable to a fixed penalty notice.

In practice notice is expected within 2 hours of commencement. The notice must state the specific reason — a vague response is not sufficient.
⚠️ FPN: £2,500 full / £1,875 discounted (pay within 29 days)

📖 s.59 — Duty to reinstate

›
💬 Plain English

Once the work is done the company must put the road back to at least the same standard it was before — properly, using the right materials and methods. They can't just dump some tarmac in the hole and leave. If the patch is badly done, too thin, wrong mix, or they never get round to the permanent fix — that's this offence.

NRSWA 1991 s.59
General duty of undertaker to reinstate

(1) An undertaker who executes street works shall reinstate the street to at least its condition before the works were executed (or better condition), and shall do so in accordance with any directions given to him by the street authority and the prescribed specifications and standards.

(2) The undertaker shall complete reinstatement within the prescribed period, and the duty to maintain the reinstatement continues for the prescribed guarantee period.

(3) An undertaker who fails to comply with this section is guilty of an offence and liable to a fixed penalty notice.

Standards set by SROH. Permanent reinstatement: 6 months (bound) or 3 months (unbound). Guarantee period: 2–3 years.
⚠️ FPN: £2,500 full / £1,875 discounted. Multiple FPNs possible for multiple openings.

📖 s.60 — Safety at the worksite

›
💬 Plain English

While work is going on the site must be made safe for everyone — pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers. Proper barriers, signs, and lights around any holes or hazards, set up correctly to the national code. If you arrive and there are no cones, no signs, an open trench with nothing round it, or the traffic management is a shambles — that's this offence.

NRSWA 1991 s.60
Safety measures

(1) An undertaker executing street works shall— (a) secure that the works are properly guarded and lit in accordance with the prescribed requirements, and (b) comply with such requirements as may be prescribed as to the use of traffic signs in connection with the works.

(2) An undertaker who fails to comply with subsection (1) is guilty of an offence and liable to a fixed penalty notice.

Requirements set by Safety at Street Works Code of Practice and Chapter 8 of the Traffic Signs Manual. Applies for the entire duration of works.
⚠️ FPN: £2,500 full / £1,875 discounted. Multiple FPNs possible. See also NCT Condition C1 (£500).

📖 s.70 — Ignoring council directions

›
💬 Plain English

The council can tell a utility company how and when to do their work — for example "you can only work between 9pm and 6am on this high street." If the company ignores a valid instruction and carries on regardless that's this offence. The council must have properly issued the direction first — verbal requests don't count.

NRSWA 1991 s.70
Directions as to timing and placing of works

(1) The street authority may give directions to an undertaker as to the time at which, or the manner in which, street works are to be executed, if the authority consider it necessary to do so— (a) for the purpose of preventing or reducing damage to the street, (b) preventing or reducing inconvenience to the public, or (c) in the interests of safety.

(2) An undertaker who fails to comply with a direction given under this section is guilty of an offence and liable to a fixed penalty notice.

Direction must be validly issued and formally served before this FPN can be used. Retain a copy of the direction as evidence.
⚠️ FPN: £2,500 full / £1,875 discounted (pay within 29 days)

📖 s.74 — Overrunning Works & Completion Notices

›
💬 Plain English

Section 74 is really two separate things that people often confuse:

1. The FPN offence — failing to give a completion notice when works are finished. That's a criminal offence carrying a £2,500 FPN. It has nothing to do with how long the works took.

2. The overrunning charges — a civil financial charge (not a criminal offence) when works take longer than they should. These are substantial — up to £10,000 per day on a busy road. These are NOT FPNs — they are daily charges invoiced by the highway authority.

Part 1 — The FPN Offence
NRSWA 1991 s.74(7B)
Failure to give completion notice

An undertaker shall give the street authority notice as soon as the works are completed — either a Works Clear notice (signing, lighting & guarding removed, permanent reinstatement not yet laid) or a Works Closed notice (permanent reinstatement complete, everything removed). Failure to give this notice is a criminal offence.

Works Clear noticeWhen to send
By end of next working day after SLG removed but before permanent reinstatement
Works Closed noticeWhen to send
By end of next working day after permanent reinstatement & all equipment removed
FPN penalty
£2,500 / £1,875 discounted
91-day limit
Yes — from date notice should have been given
📌 The FPN is for failing to send the notice — not for overrunning. An undertaker who overruns but sends their notices correctly is not liable to this FPN (but is liable to overrunning charges — see Part 2 below).
Part 2 — Overrunning Charges (Civil — not an FPN)
💬 What triggers an overrunning charge?

Works are overrunning when they last longer than either:
• The prescribed period (set by the 2009 Regulations based on works type), OR
• The reasonable period (agreed between undertaker and authority, or determined by arbitration)
— whichever is the longer. The charge runs for each day (or part day) of overrun.

Prescribed period — Minor works
3 working days
Prescribed period — Standard works
10 working days
Prescribed period — Major works
As specified in the notice
Prescribed period — Emergency/Urgent
As soon as reasonably practicable
Reasonable period
Agreed between undertaker & authority — or determined by arbitration if disputed

Key Rules & Edge Cases
When do charges start?
The day after the prescribed/reasonable period expires — charged per day or part day
When do works "end" for s.74?
Date of Works Clear or Works Closed notice — whichever is given first
Carriageway testWhat triggers higher carriageway rate?
If works occupy ANY part of the carriageway AT ANY TIME during the overrun period — even briefly
Street categoryWhich category applies?
Category at time of original notice/permit application — NOT when overrun begins
Traffic sensitive timeDoes it matter what time of day?
Higher rate if street IS traffic-sensitive — regardless of time of day during overrun
HA invoicing deadlineWhen must the authority bill?
Within 3 months of receiving Works Clear/Closed notice — or charges cannot be levied
Who can be charged?
Statutory undertakers only — NOT highway authority's own works (s.74 does not apply to HA)
Remedial works
Charged at same category as the original works being remedied
The 5-Item SLG Rule — Important Concession
💬 The single item / 5-item rule (2012 Amendment)

If works have been properly completed on time but up to 5 items of signing, lighting or guarding (SLG) have been left behind in genuine error — the overrunning charge is reduced to a single flat payment of £100, provided the undertaker removes the items by the end of the following working day after being requested to do so.

This does NOT apply if the works themselves have not been completed — only where the works are done and a small number of SLG items have been left behind. More than 5 items = full daily charges apply.

Exemptions & Defences
Revised duration noticeUndertaker can extend the period
Must notify HA before prescribed period expires — gives revised estimate. HA has prescribed time to object.
Unforeseen circumstancesDefence for overrun
If overrun caused by matters not previously foreseen or reasonably foreseeable — undertaker may submit revised estimate
HA discretionAuthority can reduce/waive
HA may reduce or waive charges in any particular case or class of case
SLG moved off highwayEquipment off road = no overrun
SLG moved off the public highway entirely = works have ended for s.74 purposes
SLG moved within highwayAwaiting collection
SLG moved to another part of the highway awaiting collection = overrun continues
⚠️ The road markings trap: Missing road markings count as works not complete for s.74 purposes. If the permanent surface is down but markings haven't been reinstated — the undertaker cannot validly submit a Works Closed notice. The clock keeps running. Issue a warning — the undertaker has until end of next day to reinstate markings to at least interim standard.
SI 2009/303 as amended by SI 2012/2272
Street Works (Charges for Unreasonably Prolonged Occupation of the Highway) (England) Regulations 2009 (as amended 2012)

🔍 s.74 — What Does & Doesn't Constitute an Overrun

›
💬 The core test — HAUC AN 2/2014 / Coordination Code Ch.10 para 10.9

The question is whether the undertaker has made proper endeavours to complete the reinstatement. If they genuinely have — but a defect is later found on inspection — that is NOT an overrun for s.74 purposes. If they manifestly have not made proper endeavours — that IS an overrun. The distinction matters enormously. Below is every common item and where it sits.

✅ These are NOT an overrun / not a s.74 trigger
✅ Saw cuts visible in the surface

Saw cuts are the straight cut lines you see around the edge of a reinstatement. They are part of the required edge preparation under SROH S6.8 — the undertaker must saw cut to a clean vertical edge before laying new material. Saw cuts visible in the surface prove that edge preparation has been done correctly. They are not evidence of incomplete works — they are evidence of compliant works. Saw cuts remain visible in the surface after reinstatement is complete and will be there permanently until a future overlay or resurfacing. You cannot use visible saw cuts as evidence that works are still in progress or that a Works Closed notice is invalid.

📖 SROH S6.8.6 — edge preparation requirement  |  SROH S6.4.4 — trimback and saw cutting
✅ Reinstatement found defective on subsequent inspection

If the undertaker completed the reinstatement and submitted a Works Closed notice, but a later inspection finds the reinstatement is defective (settlement, cracking, failed levels etc.) — this is not an overrun for s.74 purposes. It's a reinstatement defect — raise a C10/C11/C18 defect notice under s.72 instead. The key distinction: defective ≠ incomplete. The undertaker made proper endeavours; the reinstatement later failed. That's a guarantee period / defect issue, not an overrun.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario ONE — Coordination Code Ch.10 para 10.9
✅ SLG removed off the public highway (awaiting collection elsewhere)

If signing, lighting and guarding has been physically removed from the highway and is sitting on private land, a yard, or on a vehicle off the highway — the works have ended for s.74 purposes. It doesn't matter that the equipment hasn't been collected yet, as long as it's off the public highway.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario TWO
✅ Up to 5 SLG items left behind in genuine error — if removed by end of next working day

Where reinstatement is complete and all other equipment removed but up to 5 SLG items have been inadvertently left — the mitigation charge of £100 (not the full daily rate) applies, provided the items are removed by end of next working day after being asked. This only works if it's genuinely an error and not a pattern of behaviour. Items must not be affecting the carriageway or footway to qualify.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario THREE  |  SI 2012/2272 reg.9(7)–(9)
✅ Permanent reinstatement not yet laid — but interim is properly in place

An interim reinstatement is a valid completed state. If the undertaker has properly laid interim reinstatement, removed their SLG, and submitted a Works Clear notice correctly — that is not an overrun. The clock for s.74 runs from when the prescribed/reasonable period expires, not from when interim is laid. Interim is expected to be replaced with permanent within the timescales in the SROH, but having an interim in place is not itself evidence of an overrun.

📖 SROH S1.2 — guarantee periods  |  NRSWA s.74(2) — reasonable period
⚠️ These ARE an overrun / valid s.74 trigger
⚠️ Road markings not reinstated on permanent surface

Missing road markings = works not complete. The undertaker cannot validly submit a Works Closed notice if markings disturbed or covered during works have not been reinstated on the permanent surface. Issue an overrun warning — the undertaker has until end of next day (or first available site day if notice/permit required) to reinstate markings to at least interim standard.

However — gravity matters. Stop lines, double white centre lines, give way lines, yellow lines = serious, charge in full. Part of a cycle emblem or bus stop wording = consider mitigated charge. Markings already missing or indistinct before works = consider waiving.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario ONE  |  Coordination Code Ch.10 para 10.9 fn.1
⚠️ SLG still present on the highway — works period expired

If cones, barriers, signs or other SLG remain on the highway after the prescribed/reasonable period has expired — that's a physical overstay and attracts full daily charges. No mitigation unless it falls within the 5-item rule. Note: SLG moved to another part of the highway for later collection (still on highway) does not end the overrun — the authority may consider charging less than maximum, but it's still a chargeable overstay.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario TWO
⚠️ No attempt made at reinstatement — excavation left open or temporarily plated only

If the excavation is still open, or covered only with a road plate, and the prescribed/reasonable period has expired — this is a clear overrun. A road plate is not a reinstatement. The undertaker has manifestly not made proper endeavours to complete the reinstatement.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario ONE  |  SROH S6.1 — reinstatement methods
⚠️ Works Clear / Closed notice submitted but site manifestly not clear

If an undertaker submits a Works Clear or Works Closed notice but the site is visibly still occupied — SLG present, excavation open, no reinstatement in place — the notice can be treated as invalid and the overrun continues. The authority should document the evidence (photographs with timestamp) and notify the undertaker.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 — Coordination Code Ch.10
⚠️ More than 5 SLG items left on highway

More than 5 items of SLG remaining = full daily charges apply. The 5-item mitigation only works if it's clearly a genuine error and the count is 5 or fewer. 6 cones left = full rate.

📖 SI 2012/2272 reg.9(7) — HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario THREE
⚖️ Grey areas — apply judgement
⚖️ Temporary markings not applied at Works Clear stage

At Works Clear stage (interim in place, SLG removed) the undertaker should have replaced any disturbed road markings with temporary markings. If they haven't — this could be treated as an overrun. However, issue a warning first and give until end of next day to apply temporary markings before charging. Gravity test applies — missing stop line more serious than missing parking bay marking.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 — SROH S11.1
⚖️ Spoil, materials or plant left on highway after prescribed period

Spoil, unused materials or plant left on the highway after the period expires = the site is not clear. This is similar to SLG — if it's on the highway it counts as occupation. However, apply the same judgement as the 5-item rule: is it de minimis? A small bag of grit is different to a digger bucket and three pallets of tarmac. Document, notify, allow reasonable time to collect, then charge if not removed.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario THREE — works not fully clear
⚖️ Reinstatement in place but technically non-compliant with SROH

This is the hardest call. If a reinstatement has been laid but doesn't meet the SROH spec (wrong material, surface not flush, edge depression beyond tolerance) — is that an overrun or a defect? The answer depends on whether the undertaker made proper endeavours. If they clearly just threw in cold-lay on a Cat 1 road and left — that's not proper endeavours, treat as overrun. If they laid what appeared to be the right spec but it's failed the level test by 3mm — that's a defect, not an overrun. Use your judgement and document thoroughly.

📖 HAUC AN 2/2014 Scenario ONE  |  Coordination Code Ch.10 para 10.9
📌 Evidence is everything. HAUC AN 2/2014 is explicit: "the best evidence is personal knowledge supported by documentary evidence — photographs and works inspection reports." Time-stamped photographs, Street Manager records, and written notes of what you saw and when are what will defend or refute a charge. If you were criticised for an s.74 decision today — photograph everything, note the time, record the exact state of the site. Your observation is valid if you can evidence it.

Additional Reference
🔳 SMA — Stone Mastic Asphalt
A2.2 — Cat 0/1 high-spec, footways & cycleways
›
💬 Plain English

SMA looks similar to HRA but has a much higher stone content — almost all aggregate with a thin bitumen mastic holding it together. The surface looks very rough and open-textured, with large stones clearly visible. No rolled-in chippings like HRA — the aggregate is all in the mix. It's a premium material used on high-traffic roads (Cat 0/1) because of its high skid resistance and durability. If you see what looks like SMA on a residential street, that's a potential spec mismatch worth querying.

⬛ AC — Asphalt Concrete (Dense Macadam)
A2.3 — 6mm & 10mm close graded
›
💬 Plain English

AC (Asphalt Concrete, also called Dense Bituminous Macadam or DBM) is the most common reinstatement material you'll see day-to-day. It's smooth, dark grey/black, with small aggregate visible. The 6mm version has very fine texture; 10mm is slightly coarser. It's the workhorse for Cat 2, 3 and 4 roads and footways. The key thing to check on site: is the surface close-textured and consistent, or is it open, rough or crumbling? Open-textured AC is a sign of poor mixing or the wrong specification.

🌡️ Cold-Lay — PCSM & DSM
A2.4 — temporary & Cat 3/4 permanent only
›
💬 Plain English

Cold-lay is tarmac that comes in bags or bulk from a van — it doesn't need heating before use. You can spot it on site: it's often darker and more uniform than hot-lay, may look slightly oily or greasy when fresh, and doesn't have the same rough aggregate texture as hot-lay AC. There are two types: PCSM (Permanent Cold-lay Surfacing Material) and DSM (Deferred Set Mixture). Cold-lay has its place — but it's often misused as a permanent solution on roads where hot-lay is required.

💧 PMMA — Polymer Modified Mastic Asphalt
A2.5 — flowable material for small openings
›
💬 Plain English

PMMA is a flowable bituminous material — it gets poured into small excavations and narrow trenches where you can't compact properly with conventional equipment. It self-levels and self-compacts as it cools. You can spot it on site by its very smooth, almost shiny black finish with no visible aggregate — it looks like a smooth patch of black rubber. It's increasingly common for telecom and small cable works. The key thing to check is whether it's been used where it's permitted and whether the surface finish is flush and crack-free.

Small openings & narrow trenches (S6.5)
Road types permitted

Binder or surface course in small openings
Visual appearanceWhat to look for on site
Very smooth, shiny black — no aggregate visible. Slightly flexible feel.
Common defects
Shrinkage cracks, proud/sunken edges, debonding from edges
📌 PMMA shrinks slightly as it cools — small edge depression is common. Check against S2.2 tolerances. Debonding at the edges (peeling away from the saw cut) is a defect — S.59.

🪨 Surface Dressing
S6.4 — Cat 3/4 only, not as standard permanent reinstatement
›
💬 Plain English

Surface dressing is bitumen sprayed onto an existing surface with chippings rolled in — it's a thin treatment, not a structural layer. You'll recognise it by loose chippings on or near the surface and a rougher, more uneven texture than hot-lay asphalt. It's NOT a standard reinstatement technique — it can only be used in very specific circumstances (Cat 3/4, lower-traffic roads) and requires HA agreement. If you see what looks like surface dressing used as a reinstatement on a busy road, that's a significant spec concern.

Yes — HA must agree to use of surface dressing as reinstatement

Loose or recently-rolled chippings, bitumen spray visible, no proper depth
Common issueWhy inspectors flag it
Used on busy roads as cheap alternative to hot-lay
📌 Surface dressing provides no structural contribution — it's a surface seal only. Using it as a reinstatement where hot-lay is required = S.59 offence. Also check: loose chippings on the carriageway are a safety hazard — C6 may apply.

🪨 HRA Chipping Distribution
Carriageway & footway/cycleway spec
›
💬 Plain English

HRA (Hot Rolled Asphalt) is the dark, rough-textured tarmac with visible grey/white stone chips rolled into the surface. The chips are what give it its skid resistance — without them, it's just smooth black matrix with no grip. When checking chipping distribution on site, you're looking for even coverage — stones shouldn't be bunched in some areas and absent in others.

✂️ Trimback & Edge Preparation
S6.8 / S3.1 — saw cutting requirements
›
💬 Plain English

Before reinstatement, the edges of the excavation must be cut back cleanly with a saw — not just broken off. The cut edge must be vertical and straight. If you can see a ragged, broken or tapered edge at the joint between the new and existing material, the edge preparation was not done correctly. This is one of the most common causes of interface cracking and joint failure.

MethodHow to cut the edge
Saw cut — vertical, clean
Trimback distanceMinimum saw cut from excavation edge
To sound material
Long trench — projectionSaw cut extends beyond excavation edge
250mm minimum
Edge profileWhat the edge should look like
Vertical, straight or regularised — parallel to trench
CornersSmall patch / excavation corners
Avoid sharp internal corners — rounded or angled to improve compaction
Tack coatRequired after saw cutting?
Yes — bituminous emulsion on cut faces
📌 No saw cut = S.59 offence. Broken/tapered edges are the leading cause of interface cracking within the guarantee period. Retain photographs of the cut edge as evidence.

🔩 Small Openings & Narrow Trenches
S6.5 — different rules apply
›
💬 Plain English

Small openings (under a certain area) and narrow trenches (under a certain width) have different reinstatement rules. Telecom ducts, small cable pulls and service connections often fall into this category. The compaction method and material options are different — you can't always use a vibrating plate in a narrow trench, so the spec accounts for this.

💬 Plain English

Micro trenching is increasingly common — a narrow, shallow cut in the road surface used to lay fibre optic cables and telecoms ducts without a deep excavation. It's a different beast from a standard trench and has its own specific rules. Key things to check: the cut width, the fill material (must be approved), and the surface reinstatement (must match surrounding surface).

⬛ SMA — Stone Mastic Asphalt
A2.2 — high-stone content, Cat 0/1 primary material
›
💬 Plain English

SMA is a premium surface material with a very high stone content — typically around 70–75% coarse aggregate. On site it looks darker and coarser than standard tarmac, with a rough, open texture and visible angular stone. It's the required surface material on Cat 0 and Cat 1 roads because of its excellent durability and skid resistance. If you see a smooth, relatively featureless black surface on a busy A road where SMA should be, that's a red flag.

Key thing to look for: the aggregate size must match the existing surface. Hand-laying SMA requires 10mm nominal size — you can't hand-lay 14mm or 20mm SMA without HA agreement.

⬛ AC — Asphalt Concrete (Dense Macadam)
A2.3 — AC6 / AC10 — workhorse surface material
›
💬 Plain English

AC (Asphalt Concrete) — also called dense macadam — is the standard surface material for most reinstatements on Cat 2, 3 and 4 roads and footways. On site it looks like a relatively smooth, dark grey-black surface with a fairly uniform fine texture. AC10 (10mm aggregate) is the standard carriageway spec. AC6 (6mm aggregate, finer texture) is standard for footways and is also used for hand laying where AC10 would be too coarse.

Critical rule: AC10 can spill into a footway for up to 10 linear metres or 4m² — beyond that, AC6 must be used. If you see AC10 covering a large footway area, check the dimensions.

🌡️ Cold-Lay — PCSM & DSM
A2.4 — where it's permitted and where it isn't
›
💬 Plain English

Cold-lay is tarmac that comes in bags or a lorry and is applied at ambient temperature — no hot plant needed. There are two types: PCSM (Permanent Cold-lay Surfacing Material) which is approved for use as a permanent surface on lower-category roads, and DSM (Deferred Set Mixture) which is an interim/temporary material only.

The key on-site question is: is this cold-lay material being used where it's actually permitted? Cold-lay on a Cat 0, 1 or 2 carriageway as a permanent surface is a spec breach. It looks different from hot-lay — typically darker, more uniform, and slightly duller in appearance without the aggregate texture of HRA or SMA.

⚠️ May 2025 addendum: check the SROH addendum for any updates to cold-lay permissions — there were changes to DSM rules in May 2025.

🧪 PMMA — Polymer Modified Mastic Asphalt
A2.5 — flowable material for small openings
›
💬 Plain English

PMMA is a flowable material — it's poured or pumped in rather than compacted. On site it looks very smooth and uniform, typically dark grey-black with a glassy or slightly shiny surface and fine texture. No stone chips visible. It's designed for small openings and narrow trenches where you physically can't get compaction equipment in.

Key things to check: it must be flush with the surrounding surface — any proud or sunken PMMA is a fail. And it must only be used in the situations the spec permits — primarily small openings and narrow trenches on any road category.

🪨 Surface Dressing
A2 / S6.4 — only permitted on Cat 3 & 4
›
💬 Plain English

Surface dressing is a bitumen spray followed by loose chippings rolled into it — it's a surface treatment rather than a structural layer. On site it looks like a layer of loose or embedded stones on a bitumen base, often with areas where stones have been picked off by traffic. It's the cheapest surface treatment and is only permitted as a reinstatement on roads where surface dressing is the existing surface treatment — and only on the lowest traffic categories.

The most common enforcement issue: surface dressing used on a Cat 0, 1 or 2 road where asphalt is required. That is a clear materials spec breach.

NOT permitted — asphalt required

🔨 Compaction Requirements
S10 — what equipment, how many passes
›
💬 Plain English

Proper compaction is what makes a reinstatement last. If the layers aren't compacted enough, they'll settle under traffic and the surface will sink. Common site failures: wrong equipment for the material, layers too thick to compact properly, or compaction done too quickly. If you see a gang using a hand rammer on a main road subbase where a vibrating plate should be used — that's a potential spec breach.

Granular sub-baseRequired compaction method
Vibrating plate or roller
Max layer thickness — granularBefore compaction
150mm per layer
Bituminous layersCompaction method
Vibrating plate or roller
Max bituminous liftSurface/binder course compaction depth
See A2.8 table
Hand rammerWhen is hand rammer acceptable?
Narrow trenches <300mm only
Concrete / rigidCompaction method
Vibrotamper, poker vibrator or equivalent

Surface Material Reference
🟫 SMA — Stone Mastic Asphalt
A2.2 — high-performance surface course
›
💬 What it looks like on site

SMA has a very distinctive appearance — very high stone content, closely packed aggregate that's almost touching, with a dark binder just visible between the stones. It doesn't have rolled-in chippings like HRA — the stones are in the mix itself. On a reinstatement, the patch should match this texture closely. A smooth, fine-textured surface on an SMA road is wrong material.

Where usedRoad categories
Cat 0 & 1 (required), Cat 2–4 (permitted)
Cat 0 & 1 mixes
SMA 14, SMA 10, SMA 6 (HA approval req.)
Footways & cycle tracks
SMA 6 surf 40/60, 70/100 or 100/150
Hand laying — aggregate sizeSpecial rule
Must use 10mm even if existing is 20mm or 14mm
Wheel tracking Cat 0/1
Classification 2 mandatory
SMA with PMB — hand laying
By HA agreement only
📌 The aggregate size must match the existing surface (with the hand-laying exception above). Using the wrong mix spec on Cat 0/1 is a C18 breach even if the surface looks acceptable.

⬛ AC — Asphalt Concrete / Dense Macadam
A2.3 — 6mm & 10mm close-graded surface course
›
💬 What it looks like on site

Dense macadam / asphalt concrete is the most commonly used reinstatement material — the standard black tarmac most people think of. The surface is relatively smooth with visible fine aggregate, no individual large stones or chippings sitting on top. A 6mm mix has a finer, smoother texture; 10mm is slightly coarser. Look for an even, dense surface with no open voids, ravelling or loose material. A good AC surface is consistent in colour and texture across the whole patch.

All carriageway types — standard mix
AC10 close surf 100/150
Footways & cycle tracks — preferred
AC6 dense surf 100/150
Footways — AC10 from carriageway worksMaximum extent into footway
Max 10m linear or 4m²
Bitumen grade
100/150 penetration
Cat 0 & 1 roadsIs AC acceptable?
Alternative only — HRA or SMA preferred
📌 AC on a Cat 0/1 road as the sole surface course is a potential spec issue — check whether HRA or SMA was the original surface. On Cat 2–4 it is standard. AC10 may extend into footway from carriageway works up to the limits above — beyond that, HA agreement required.

🌡️ Cold-Lay — PCSM & DSM
A2.4 — where permitted and where not
›
💬 What it looks like on site

Cold-lay comes out of a bag or small van — no hot mix plant required. It's commonly used as a temporary fix. You can usually spot it because it looks different to the surrounding road — often darker, sometimes slightly shiny, with a very uniform fine texture and no visible aggregate variation. It's softer in warm weather. The key question on site: is this being used as a permanent surface where it's not permitted?

PCSM — permanent use permitted
Cat 3 & 4 carriageways, footways B/C/D
PCSM — NOT permitted as permanent
Cat 0, 1 & 2 carriageways
DSM (deferred set)
Interim reinstatement only — must be replaced
As interim — all categories
Permitted everywhere as temporary patch
Narrow trenches Cat 2Special case
PCSM permitted with wheel tracking class 2
📌 Cold-lay as permanent on Cat 0, 1 or 2 = C18 / S.59. Beyond interim deadline = C10 also applies. A May 2025 addendum updated cold-lay guidance — check the HAUC addendum link below for latest.

🧪 PMMA — Polymer Modified Mastic Asphalt
A2.5 — flowable material, small openings
›
💬 What it looks like on site

PMMA is poured or pumped — not compacted. On site it looks very smooth and uniform, often slightly glossier than conventional asphalt. It flows around obstacles like valve boxes without needing compaction equipment. Most often seen in small openings and narrow trenches. A correctly laid PMMA surface should be flush with the surrounding road and have no visible voids or pull-back at the edges.

Permitted use
Small openings & narrow trenches (S6.5)
Road categories
All road categories
Compaction
Not required — flowable, self-levels
Position in layers
Binder or surface course in small openings
Surface finish check
Must be flush — no proud edges or voids
📌 PMMA used outside small openings may be outside spec. The surface must still meet S2.2 (levels) and S2.4 (regularity) tolerances despite being flowable.

🪨 Surface Dressing
S6.4 — limited permitted use only
›
💬 What it looks like on site

Surface dressing is a thin treatment — bituminous binder sprayed on the existing surface with chippings rolled in. It's not a structural material. On site it looks like loose stones initially, or a thin chipped surface once trafficked. The question is whether it's acceptable as a permanent surface course for this road type. On most roads it isn't — using it where hot-lay is required is a clear spec breach.

Permitted for reinstatement on
Cat 3 & 4 only
NOT permitted on
Cat 0, 1 & 2 — not acceptable
Additional condition
Only where existing surface was surface dressing
Chipping size
Must match existing surface dressing
Footways
Not permitted on footways
📌 Surface dressing on a Cat 0/1/2 road = S.59 / C18. Even on Cat 3/4 it's only acceptable where the existing surface was already surface dressing. A surface-dressed reinstatement on an asphalt road is wrong regardless of road category.
